cse-2015-2-cs-36.approach: Recall the design technique behind each classic algorithm: Dijkstra picks the closest unvisited vertex (greedy), Floyd–Warshall builds on subproblems over intermediate vertices (DP), binary search halves the range (divide and conquer), and backtracking explores depth-first.

steps.body:
| Algorithm | Paradigm |
|---|---|
| 1. Dijkstra | iii. Greedy — always settle the vertex with the smallest tentative distance |
| 2. Floyd–Warshall | ii. DP — $d_k(i,j) = \min(d_{k-1}(i,j),\ d_{k-1}(i,k)+d_{k-1}(k,j))$ |
| 3. Binary search | i. Divide and conquer — recurse on one half |
| 4. Backtracking | iv. DFS — extend a partial solution as deep as possible, undo on failure |

cse-2015-2-cs-44.approach: Draw the cycle-by-cycle chart. PO is a single stage, so DIV waits for MUL to leave PO; forwarding from PO lets a dependent instruction execute PO in the cycle right after its producer's last PO cycle.
cse-2015-2-cs-44.given:
| Instr | PO cycles | Depends on |
|---|---|---|
| MUL | 3 | — |
| DIV | 5 | — |
| ADD | 1 | R5 (MUL), R6 (DIV) |
| SUB | 1 | R7 (ADD) |

steps.title: MUL
steps.body: IF in 1, OF in 2, PO in 3–5, WB in 6.

steps.title: DIV waits for the PO unit
steps.body: IF 2, OF 3. PO is busy with MUL until cycle 5, so DIV stalls in 4–5, executes PO in 6–10 and WB in 11.

steps.title: ADD needs R6
steps.body: R6 is produced at the end of cycle 10 and forwarded from PO, so ADD's PO is in cycle 11 and WB in 12 (R5 was ready long before).

steps.title: SUB needs R7
steps.body:
R7 is forwarded from ADD's PO (cycle 11), so SUB's PO is in cycle 12 and WB in 13.

Total = **13** clock cycles.

pitfalls: Letting DIV's PO overlap MUL's PO (assumes multiple execution units).
Waiting for WB before reading the operand — forwarding avoids that.
cse-2015-2-cs-44.verification: Last instruction finishes at cycle $10\ (\text{DIV PO ends}) + 1\ (\text{ADD PO}) + 1\ (\text{SUB PO}) + 1\ (\text{SUB WB}) = 13$.

steps.body: Elements `a[0..left_end-1]` are $\le$ pivot and there are `left_end` of them. The $k$-th smallest is among them with the same rank: `kth_smallest(a, left_end, k)`.

steps.body:
The right part starts at `a + left_end + 1` and has $n - (\text{left\_end}+1)$ elements. The `left_end+1` elements before it are all smaller, so the rank becomes $k - \text{left\_end} - 1$:
`kth_smallest(a+left_end+1, n-left_end-1, k-left_end-1)` → option (A).

Second call starts at `a`, i.e. searches the left part again instead of the right part.

cse-2015-2-cs-48.approach: The intended model treats each full adder as a black box whose worst-case delay is 4.8 µs (two XORs for the sum, XOR+AND+OR for the carry), and the ripple-carry adder as four of them in series: $4 \times 4.8 = 19.2$ µs.

steps.title: Gate delays
steps.body: AND/OR = 1.2 µs, XOR = $2 \times 1.2 = 2.4$ µs.

steps.title: Delay of one full adder
steps.body:
Sum $= (A \oplus B) \oplus C_{in}$: two XORs in series → $2.4 + 2.4 = 4.8$ µs.
Carry $= AB + C_{in}(A\oplus B)$: XOR → AND → OR $= 2.4 + 1.2 + 1.2 = 4.8$ µs.
So one full adder takes 4.8 µs.

pitfalls: A strict gate-level analysis lets later stages compute $A \oplus B$ in parallel, so each later carry adds only AND+OR = 2.4 µs: $4.8 + 2.4 + 2.4 + 2.4 = 12$ µs. The widely cited key uses the simpler 4 × 4.8 model.
cse-2015-2-cs-48.verification: Black-box model: 4 stages × 4.8 µs = 19.2 µs. The gate-level critical path gives 12 µs, so the record is flagged for review.
